claim: The World Health Organization has included three bunyaviruses on the Blueprint list of viruses likely to cause major epidemics and for which no, or insufficient countermeasures exist.
source: The World Health Organization has included three bunyaviruses posing an increasing threat to human health on the Blueprint list of viruses likely to cause major epidemics and for which no, or insufficient countermeasures exist.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to WHO's Blueprint list, which is established scientific knowledge about priority pathogens.

claim: VHH building blocks were assembled into highly potent neutralizing complexes using bacterial superglue technology.
source: VHH building blocks were assembled into highly potent neutralizing complexes using bacterial superglue technology.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multimeric complexes reduced and prevented virus-induced morbidity and mortality in mice upon prophylactic administration.
source: The multimeric complexes were shown to reduce and prevent virus-induced morbidity and mortality in mice upon prophylactic administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Bispecific molecules engineered to present two different VHHs fused to an Fc domain were effective upon therapeutic administration.
source: Bispecific molecules engineered to present two different VHHs fused to an Fc domain were further shown to be effective upon therapeutic administration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from therapeutic treatment experiments.

claim: RVFV is prioritized by the World Health Organization as being likely to cause major epidemics for which no, or insufficient countermeasures exist.
source: Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), a phlebovirus within the order Bunyavirales, is prioritized by the World Health Organization (WHO) as being likely to cause major epidemics for which no, or insufficient countermeasures exist.
evidence: This is supported by reference to WHO prioritization, which is established knowledge.

claim: RVFV is currently confined to the African continent, the Arabian Peninsula and several islands off the coast of Southern Africa.
source: RVFV is currently confined to the African continent, the Arabian Peninsula and several islands off the coast of Southern Africa, where it causes recurrent outbreaks (Clark et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Clark et al., 2018.

claim: The world-wide distribution of competent mosquito vectors and susceptible animals underscores the risk for RVFV emergence in currently unaffected areas.
source: The world-wide distribution of competent mosquito vectors and susceptible animals underscores the risk for emergence in currently unaffected areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of vectors and susceptible hosts.

claim: RVFV causes major epizootics among livestock, characterized by abortion storms and large-scale mortality among newborn ruminants in endemic areas.
source: In endemic areas, RVFV causes major epizootics among livestock, characterized by abortion storms and large-scale mortality among newborn ruminants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RVFV disease manifestations in livestock.

claim: RVFV infects humans either through direct contact with infected animal tissues or via the bites of infected mosquitoes.
source: Importantly, the virus also infects humans, either through direct contact with infected animal tissues or via the bites of infected mosquitoes (Hartman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hartman, 2017.

claim: RVFV-infected individuals generally present with mild to severe flu-like symptoms, however a minority of patients may develop encephalitis or hemorrhagic fever.
source: Infected individuals generally present with mild to severe flu-like symptoms, however a minority of patients may develop encephalitis or hemorrhagic fever.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RVFV clinical manifestations in humans.

claim: In 2011, the incursion of Schmallenberg virus (SBV) in Europe demonstrated that orthobunyaviruses are capable of spreading very efficiently across new territories.
source: In 2011, the incursion of Schmallenberg virus (SBV) in Europe demonstrated that orthobunyaviruses are capable of spreading very efficiently across new territories.
evidence: This is a historical observation about SBV spread, representing established knowledge.

claim: SBV infections are associated with fever and reduced milk production in cows and severe malformations in offspring of both large and small ruminants.
source: SBV infections are associated with fever and reduced milk production in cows and severe malformations in offspring of both large and small ruminants (Hoffmann et al., 2012; van den Brom et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2012 and van den Brom et al., 2012.

claim: SBV is categorized as a biosafety level-2 pathogen and is not pathogenic to humans.
source: SBV is categorized as a biosafety level-2 pathogen and is not pathogenic to humans, facilitating its use as a model of zoonotic orthobunyaviruses that require a higher level of containment (Golender et al., 2015; van Eeden et al., 2014; van Eeden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Golender et al., 2015; van Eeden et al., 2014; van Eeden et al., 2012.

claim: No effective antiviral therapy is available to treat bunyavirus infections in humans.
source: At the moment, no effective antiviral therapy is available to treat bunyavirus infections in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of bunyavirus therapeutics.

claim: Patients with bunyavirus infections essentially rely on supportive care.
source: Patients essentially rely on supportive care.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current treatment options for bunyavirus infections.

claim: Some promising pre-clinical and clinical data have been obtained with small molecules, mainly nucleoside analogues, that interfere with viral replication.
source: Some promising pre-clinical and clinical data have been obtained with small molecules, mainly nucleoside analogues, that interfere with viral replication (Gowen and Hickerson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gowen and Hickerson, 2017.

claim: Recent X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy/tomography data have provided novel insights into the bunyavirus glycoprotein architecture.
source: Recent X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy/tomography data have provided novel insights into the bunyavirus glycoprotein architecture that may facilitate the development of bunyavirus antibody therapies in the future (Wu et al., 2017b; Hellert et al., 2019; Halldorsson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2017b; Hellert et al., 2019; Halldorsson et al., 2018.

claim: After vaccines, antibody therapies are considered the most effective tools to fight (re)emerging life-threatening viral infections.
source: After vaccines, antibody therapies are considered the most effective tools to fight (re)emerging life-threatening viral infections (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2017.

claim: In only a few species such as camelids and nurse sharks, heavy chain-only antibodies (HCAbs) are found.
source: Interestingly, in only a few species such as camelids and nurse sharks, heavy chain-only antibodies (HCAbs) are found, of which the antigen binding domain can be expressed as a single-domain antibody (sdAb) (Arbabi-Ghahroudi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arbabi-Ghahroudi, 2017.

claim: Camelid derived sdAbs are known as VHHs.
source: Camelid derived sdAbs, known as VHHs, are increasingly used as tools in medicine, including virus neutralization (Wu et al., 2017a; De Vlieger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHH nomenclature, also supported by citations.

claim: VHHs are intrinsically highly soluble molecules.
source: VHHs are intrinsically highly soluble molecules and due to their distinctive structure with extended antigen-binding CDR3 region and overall small size, some are able to target unique (cryptic) antigenic sites not accessible to conventional antibodies (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Muyldermans, 2013.

claim: Some VHHs are able to target unique (cryptic) antigenic sites not accessible to conventional antibodies due to their distinctive structure with extended antigen-binding CDR3 region and overall small size.
source: VHHs are intrinsically highly soluble molecules and due to their distinctive structure with extended antigen-binding CDR3 region and overall small size, some are able to target unique (cryptic) antigenic sites not accessible to conventional antibodies (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Muyldermans, 2013.

claim: VHHs with nanomolar or even picomolar affinity targeting a broad spectrum of antigens have been described.
source: VHHs with nanomolar or even picomolar affinity targeting a broad spectrum of antigens have been described (Jin et al., 2017; Arbabi-Ghahroudi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2017 and Arbabi-Ghahroudi, 2017.

claim: The single-domain nature of VHHs allows easy genetic manipulation and favors efficient expression in various heterologous systems including microorganisms.
source: The single-domain nature additionally allows easy genetic manipulation and favors efficient expression in various heterologous systems including microorganisms (Harmsen and De Haard, 2007a; Liu and Huang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harmsen and De Haard, 2007a and Liu and Huang, 2018.

claim: A multimeric VHH has shown great promise in counteracting severe pulmonary disease in infants caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
source: With respect to virus neutralization, a multimeric VHH has shown great promise in counteracting severe pulmonary disease in infants caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) (Detalle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Detalle et al., 2016.

claim: The therapeutic potency of multivalent or multispecific VHH complexes is explained by their improved avidity, selectivity and kinetics compared to individual VHHs.
source: The therapeutic potency of complexes consisting of multimers of the same VHH (multivalent) or combinations of VHHs targeting different antigenic sites (multispecific) is explained by their improved avidity, selectivity and kinetics compared to individual VHHs (Hultberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hultberg et al., 2011.

claim: Selection of the optimal VHH combination and optimal VHH formats is still challenging.
source: Although techniques to use VHHs as building blocks to generate multifunctional molecules are well established, selection of the optimal VHH combination and optimal VHH formats is still challenging (Iezzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iezzi et al., 2018.

claim: The discovery of 'bacterial superglues' has enabled the creation of unique protein architectures.
source: Recently, the discovery of 'bacterial superglues' has enabled the creation of unique protein architectures.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial superglue technology.

claim: Bacterial superglues are comprised of a bacterially-derived peptide and a small protein able to form unbreakable isopeptide bonds.
source: The superglues are comprised of a bacterially-derived peptide and a small protein able to form unbreakable isopeptide bonds (Veggiani et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Veggiani et al., 2014.

claim: The first bacterial superglue was developed by splitting the immunoglobulin-like collagen adhesion domain (CnaB2) of the fibronectin binding protein (FbaB) of Streptococcus pyogenes into SpyTag and SpyCatcher.
source: The first bacterial superglue was developed by splitting the immunoglobulin-like collagen adhesion domain (CnaB2) of the fibronectin binding protein (FbaB) of Streptococcus pyogenes (Zakeri et al., 2012) into a peptide and a protein fragment referred to as SpyTag and SpyCatcher.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zakeri et al., 2012.

claim: When SpyTag and SpyCatcher meet, an amide bond is formed which is highly specific and irreversible.
source: When the two peptides meet, an amide bond is formed which is highly specific and irreversible.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SpyTag/SpyCatcher mechanism.

claim: Covalent bond formation between SpyTag and SpyCatcher occurs within minutes upon mixing and is highly robust under various conditions.
source: Covalent bond formation occurs within minutes upon mixing and is highly robust under various conditions (Zakeri et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zakeri et al., 2012.

claim: Llamas were inoculated with the live-attenuated RVFV vaccine strain Clone 13, RVFV virus-like particles (VLPs) or SBV NL-F6.
source: To obtain a source of RVFV and SBV-specific VHHs with potential neutralizing activity for the respective viruses, llamas were inoculated with the live-attenuated RVFV vaccine strain Clone 13, RVFV virus-like particles (VLPs) or SBV NL-F6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: All inoculated llamas responded well with virus-specific neutralizing antibodies in serum above a 50% neutralizing titer of 500.
source: All inoculated animals responded well with virus-specific neutralizing antibodies in serum above a 50% neutralizing titer of 500 (Figure 1B; Wichgers Schreur et al., 2017; Loeffen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Wichgers Schreur et al., 2017 and Loeffen et al., 2012.

claim: The B-cell-derived VHH phagemid libraries contained >10^7 unique clones per animal.
source: The B-cell-derived VHH phagemid libraries contained >107 unique clones per animal.
evidence: This is experimental data about the library diversity.

claim: 62 unique RVFV-Gnecto-specific clones that grouped into 16 CDR groups (15 CDR3 groups) were identified.
source: In total 62 unique RVFV-Gnecto-specific clones that grouped into 16 CDR groups (15 CDR3 groups) and 15 unique SBV-Gchead-specific clones that grouped into 6 CDR3 groups were identified (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data about VHH selection, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 15 unique SBV-Gchead-specific clones that grouped into 6 CDR3 groups were identified.
source: In total 62 unique RVFV-Gnecto-specific clones that grouped into 16 CDR groups (15 CDR3 groups) and 15 unique SBV-Gchead-specific clones that grouped into 6 CDR3 groups were identified (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data about VHH selection, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The RVFV VHH panel (N = 16) was shown to target three independent antigenic sites within RVFV-Gnecto, referred to as the red, blue and yellow antigenic sites.
source: The RVFV VHH panel (N = 16) was shown to target three independent antigenic sites within RVFV-Gnecto, referred to as the red, blue and yellow antigenic sites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from competition ELISA shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All of the VHHs of the red antigenic site did not show typical sigmoidal curves, suggesting markedly reduced avidity for monomeric Gnecto.
source: When compared to the VHHs of the blue and the yellow antigenic sites, all of the VHHs of the red antigenic site did not show typical sigmoidal curves, suggesting markedly reduced avidity for monomeric Gnecto (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The yellow antigenic site, which is targeted by RV104, RV136 and RV148, is located on subdomain B of RVFV-Gn.
source: The results show that the yellow antigenic site, which is targeted by RV104, RV136 and RV148, is located on subdomain B and that the blue antigenic site, recognized by RV107 and RV115, is primarily located on the β-ribbon domain.
evidence: This is experimental data from subdomain mapping experiments.

claim: The blue antigenic site, recognized by RV107 and RV115, is primarily located on the β-ribbon domain of RVFV-Gn.
source: The results show that the yellow antigenic site, which is targeted by RV104, RV136 and RV148, is located on subdomain B and that the blue antigenic site, recognized by RV107 and RV115, is primarily located on the β-ribbon domain.
evidence: This is experimental data from subdomain mapping experiments.

claim: The red antigenic site could not be mapped to a specific subdomain, suggesting that this site is present at a subdomain interface.
source: The red antigenic site could not be mapped to a specific subdomain, suggesting that this site is present at a subdomain interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental mapping data.

claim: SB11 and SB14 target the same antigenic site as mAb 1C11 at the apical end of the SBV Gc head domain.
source: Competition ELISAs with 1C11 and 4B6 and our SBV VHH panel suggests that SB11 and SB14 target the same antigenic site as 1C11 at the apical end of the domain, whereas no competition was observed with 4B6 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on competition ELISA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An SB10 escape mutant carries the single point mutation Y541C located directly at the head domain's contact area with the stalk.
source: For SB10, of which the antigenic site is independent from the others, we generated an escape mutant carrying the single point mutation Y541C located directly at the head domain's contact area with the stalk (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This is experimental data from escape mutant selection shown in Figure 2E and 2G.

claim: At nM range concentrations, no neutralization was observed for any of the monovalent VHHs.
source: At nM range concentrations, no neutralization was observed for any of the monovalent VHHs (Figure 3; left panel of the figure and diagonal set of bars).
evidence: This is experimental data from virus neutralization tests shown in Figure 3.

claim: Combining two VHHs in the VNT assays resulted in moderate neutralization for some SBV VHH combinations (ND50 around 200 nM) whereas still no neutralization was observed for RVFV VHH mixtures.
source: Combining two VHHs in the VNT assays resulted in moderate neutralization for some SBV VHH combinations (ND50 around 200 nM) whereas still no neutralization was observed for RVFV VHH mixtures (Figure 3; left part of the figure with double colored bars).
evidence: This is experimental data from virus neutralization tests shown in Figure 3.

claim: Several multimeric complexes very efficiently neutralized with ND50 <10 nM.
source: The VNT assays subsequently revealed that several multimeric complexes very efficiently neutralized with ND50 <10 nM (Figure 3; middle and right panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from virus neutralization tests shown in Figure 3.

claim: For RVFV, targeting of two distinct antigenic sites seemed a prerequisite to enable efficient neutralization.
source: For RVFV, targeting of two distinct antigenic sites seemed a prerequisite to enable efficient neutralization (Figure 3A), whereas for SBV both bivalent and bispecific complexes were capable of neutralization (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For SBV both bivalent and bispecific complexes were capable of neutralization.
source: For RVFV, targeting of two distinct antigenic sites seemed a prerequisite to enable efficient neutralization (Figure 3A), whereas for SBV both bivalent and bispecific complexes were capable of neutralization (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The length of the scaffolds did not have a major effect on neutralization efficiency of the RVFV VHH complexes.
source: Interestingly, the length of the scaffolds did not have a major effect on neutralization efficiency of the RVFV VHH complexes, whereas the length did influence efficacy of the SBV complexes.
evidence: This is an observation based on experimental data from neutralization assays.

claim: The length of scaffolds influenced efficacy of the SBV complexes, with complexes based on the ELP3 scaffold (the longest tested) showing markedly higher neutralization efficiencies.
source: Interestingly, the length of the scaffolds did not have a major effect on neutralization efficiency of the RVFV VHH complexes, whereas the length did influence efficacy of the SBV complexes. Complexes based on the ELP3 scaffold (the longest tested) showed markedly higher neutralization efficiencies.
evidence: This is experimental data from neutralization assays comparing different scaffold lengths.

claim: Treatment with RV104-ELP2-RV107 (without ABD) could not prevent or delay morbidity and mortality in RVFV-infected mice.
source: The results of the RVFV mouse experiment showed that in the absence of the ABD domain (RV104-ELP2-RV107) morbidity and mortality could not be prevented or delayed, whereas treatment with both RV104-ELP2ABD-RV107 and RV104-ELP2ABD-RV150 resulted in a marked delay in mortality, of which the delay was most pronounced for RV104-ELP2ABD-RV107 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Treatment with RV104-ELP2ABD-RV107 and RV104-ELP2ABD-RV150 resulted in a marked delay in mortality in RVFV-infected mice.
source: The results of the RVFV mouse experiment showed that in the absence of the ABD domain (RV104-ELP2-RV107) morbidity and mortality could not be prevented or delayed, whereas treatment with both RV104-ELP2ABD-RV107 and RV104-ELP2ABD-RV150 resulted in a marked delay in mortality, of which the delay was most pronounced for RV104-ELP2ABD-RV107 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The trispecific RV104-ELP-RV150-ELPABD-RV107 complex protected RVFV-infected mice most efficiently.
source: Interestingly, the trispecific RV104-ELP-RV150-ELPABD-RV107 complex protected the mice most efficiently, thereby suggesting that targeting of up to three antigenic sites simultaneously is very effective.
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The SB10-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex prevented mortality in 5 out of 6 SBV-infected mice.
source: For SBV, the SB10-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex prevented mortality in 5 out of 6 mice whereas the SB9-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex protected all of the inoculated mice (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The SB9-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex protected all of the inoculated SBV-infected mice.
source: For SBV, the SB10-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex prevented mortality in 5 out of 6 mice whereas the SB9-ELP2ABD-SB10 complex protected all of the inoculated mice (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5J.

claim: None of the surviving SBV-infected mice treated with VHH complexes showed any clinical signs of disease or significant weight loss.
source: In both groups, none of the surviving animals showed any clinical signs of disease or significant weight loss.
evidence: This is experimental observation from mouse infection experiments.

claim: For all the antibody treated SBV-infected mice, viral RNA loads in blood and tissue samples were markedly reduced in comparison to the control animals.
source: In addition, for all the antibody treated mice viral RNA loads in blood and tissue samples were markedly reduced in comparison to the control animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efficient neutralization at ND50 <1 nM was mainly observed with the bispecific hIgG1Fc-VHH constellations.
source: In line with the ELP results, efficient neutralization at ND50 <1 nM was mainly observed with the bispecific constellations (Figure 6C) despite binding avidities to Gnecto that were highly similar (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is experimental data from neutralization assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 60-100% protection was achieved with prophylactic administration of hIgG1Fc-VHH chimeric antibodies in RVFV-infected mice.
source: The results show that 60-100% protection was achieved with prophylactic administration and, remarkably, 60% protection was achieved after therapeutic administration (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 6F and 6G.

claim: 60% protection was achieved after therapeutic administration of hIgG1Fc-VHH chimeric antibodies in RVFV-infected mice.
source: The results show that 60-100% protection was achieved with prophylactic administration and, remarkably, 60% protection was achieved after therapeutic administration (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 6F and 6G.

claim: The lack of knowledge about bunyavirus glycoprotein structures and immunogenic domains together with rudimentary knowledge on mechanisms of neutralization have hampered the development of antibody-based bunyavirus therapies.
source: The lack of knowledge about bunyavirus glycoprotein structures and immunogenic domains together with rudimentary knowledge on mechanisms of neutralization, have hampered the development of antibody-based bunyavirus therapies.
evidence: This is an inference about the historical state of the field.

claim: Novel structural data on the glycoproteins, obtained from combined X-ray and cryo-electron microscopy/tomography of whole virions for some members of the Bunyavirales provide exciting new opportunities.
source: However, novel structural data on the glycoproteins, obtained from combined X-ray and cryo-electron microscopy/tomography of whole virions for some members of the Bunyavirales provide now exciting new opportunities (Wu et al., 2017b; Hellert et al., 2019; Halldorsson et al., 2018; Allen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2017b; Hellert et al., 2019; Halldorsson et al., 2018; Allen et al., 2018.

claim: A major advantage of the presented approach over more conventional approaches is the modularity and subsequent flexibility and directionality in complex construction.
source: A major advantage of the presented approach over more conventional approaches is the modularity and subsequent flexibility and directionality in complex construction, making selection of the most potent complexes a relatively easy task.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the method based on the experimental results.

claim: Genetic fusion of VHHs generally results in decreased production yields.
source: This modularity additionally ensures efficient production, while genetic fusion of VHHs generally results in decreased production yields.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHH production.

claim: N-terminal fusions of VHHs can decrease affinity.
source: Moreover, interference with CDRs is limited due to the flexibility in positioning of the superglue tags in the VHHs, particularly when compared to VHHs linked by genetic fusion, where N-terminal fusions can decrease affinity (Els Conrath et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Els Conrath et al., 2001.

claim: A potential disadvantage of using bacterial superglues in therapeutics is their intrinsic immunogenicity.
source: A potential disadvantage of using bacterial superglues in therapeutics is their intrinsic immunogenicity, leading to immune responses that do not contribute to protection and may even reduce efficacy, particularly with successive treatments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the approach.

claim: The synergistic effect of mixtures of antibodies targeting two or more distinct antigenic sites on RVFV virions was reported more than 25 years ago by Besselaar and Blackburn.
source: The synergistic effect of mixtures of antibodies targeting two or more distinct antigenic sites on RVFV virions was already reported more than 25 years ago by Besselaar and Blackburn (1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Besselaar and Blackburn, 1992.

claim: Conventional non-neutralizing RVFV monoclonal antibodies efficiently neutralized when they were used in combination.
source: They showed that conventional non-neutralizing RVFV monoclonal antibodies efficiently neutralized when they were used in combination (Besselaar and Blackburn, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Besselaar and Blackburn, 1992.

claim: The requirement to target more than one antigenic site for effective bunyavirus neutralization might be related to the broad range of receptor and attachment molecules used for viral attachment and entry.
source: The requirement to target more than one antigenic site for effective bunyavirus neutralization might be related to the broad range of receptor and attachment molecules used for viral attachment and entry in both insect and mammalian cells of which several are of non-proteinaceous nature (Albornoz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to Albornoz et al., 2016.

claim: Efficient neutralization by VHHs required conjugation of the VHHs to a larger scaffold.
source: Remarkably, we did not observe efficient neutralization by simply mixing VHHs targeting two distinct antigenic sites. Efficient neutralization required conjugation of the VHHs to a larger scaffold.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the study.

claim: All selected RVFV VHHs bind to the head domain of the Gn glycoprotein.
source: To gain insight into the mechanisms of RVFV neutralization, the VHHs were mapped on the Gn glycoprotein. This showed that all selected RVFV VHHs bind to the head domain of the Gn glycoprotein.
evidence: This is experimental data from mapping experiments.

claim: In the virion context, RVFV Gn forms heterodimers with Gc and assembles into capsomers that are organized into an icosahedral lattice with a T = 12 quasisymmetry.
source: In the virion context, Gn forms heterodimers with Gc and assembles into capsomers that are organized into an icosahedral lattice with a T = 12 quasisymmetry (Halldorsson et al., 2018; Sherman et al., 2009; Huiskonen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halldorsson et al., 2018; Sherman et al., 2009; Huiskonen et al., 2009.

claim: RVFV Gn is involved in receptor binding.
source: Gn is involved in receptor binding and Gc, as a class II fusion protein, is responsible for fusion of the viral membrane with the endosome (Guardado-Calvo et al., 2017; Kielian, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guardado-Calvo et al., 2017 and Kielian, 2006.

claim: RVFV Gc, as a class II fusion protein, is responsible for fusion of the viral membrane with the endosome.
source: Gn is involved in receptor binding and Gc, as a class II fusion protein, is responsible for fusion of the viral membrane with the endosome (Guardado-Calvo et al., 2017; Kielian, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guardado-Calvo et al., 2017 and Kielian, 2006.

claim: The Gc fusion peptide is shielded by Gn subdomain A (I) and the β-ribbon domain (II) to prevent premature fusion.
source: To prevent premature fusion of Gc, the Gc fusion peptide is shielded by Gn subdomain A (I) and the β-ribbon domain (II) (Halldorsson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Halldorsson et al., 2018.

claim: Binding of VHHs that target the β-ribbon domain could potentially interfere with heterodimer dissociation for fusion or with fusion loop insertion.
source: Binding of VHHs that target the β-ribbon domain (blue panel) could potentially interfere with heterodimer dissociation for fusion or with fusion loop insertion.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of neutralization.

claim: The VHHs targeting domain B most likely interfere with receptor binding.
source: The VHHs targeting domain B (yellow panel) most likely interfere with receptor binding although specific functions have yet to be identified for this domain.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of neutralization.

claim: The apical end of the SBV Gc head domain appears to be highly immunogenic in llamas.
source: The apical end of the Gc head domain thus appears to be highly immunogenic in llamas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that most VHHs target this region.

claim: The same point mutation (Y541C) found in the SB10 escape mutant was also found in an SBV field sample from a malformed goatling in 2012.
source: Intriguingly, the same point mutation was also found in an SBV field sample from a malformed goatling in 2012 (BH 233/12–1, GenBank: KC108871, Fischer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2013 and reference to GenBank sequence.

claim: Production of the two hIgG1Fc-VHH fusion proteins with the CHO cell based transient expression platform was efficient.
source: Production of the two hIgG1Fc-VHH fusion proteins with the CHO cell based transient expression platform (Daramola et al., 2014) was efficient and preliminary data suggest that the expression and purification profiles are similar to what is usually seen with conventional bispecific antibodies.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the production process, with citation to Daramola et al., 2014.

claim: Preliminary data suggest that the expression and purification profiles of hIgG1Fc-VHH fusion proteins are similar to what is usually seen with conventional bispecific antibodies.
source: Production of the two hIgG1Fc-VHH fusion proteins with the CHO cell based transient expression platform (Daramola et al., 2014) was efficient and preliminary data suggest that the expression and purification profiles are similar to what is usually seen with conventional bispecific antibodies.
evidence: This is preliminary experimental observation from the production process.

claim: VHH-based biotherapeutics hold great promise for the treatment of bunyavirus infections either prophylactically or therapeutically.
source: Altogether, these results emphasize that VHH-based biotherapeutics hold great promise for the treatment of bunyavirus infections either prophylactically or therapeutically.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: RVFV-Gnecto and SBV-Gchead are considered to be the main targets of neutralizing antibodies against the respective viruses.
source: Both RVFV-Gnecto and SBV-Gchead are considered to be the main targets of neutralizing antibodies against the respective viruses (Hellert et al., 2019; Wernike et al., 2017; Roman-Sosa et al., 2017; Kortekaas et al., 2010; Kortekaas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hellert et al., 2019; Wernike et al., 2017; Roman-Sosa et al., 2017; Kortekaas et al., 2010; Kortekaas et al., 2012.

claim: Binding of a VHH complex to circulating albumin is expected to extend the half-life due to an increased size of the complex and recycling through the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).
source: Binding of a VHH complex to circulating albumin is expected to extend the half-life not only due to an increased size of the complex, but also as a result of recycling through the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) (Mehand et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge, supported by citations to Mehand et al., 2018 and Jacobs et al., 2015.

claim: Crystal structures of the SBV Gc head domain in complex with two neutralizing murine mAbs showed that 1C11 binds to the apical end of the head domain, near the N686 glycosylation site.
source: Crystal structures of the head domain in complex with two neutralizing murine mAbs, referred to as 1C11 and 4B6, have recently shown that 1C11 binds to the apical end of the head domain, near the N686 glycosylation site, and that 4B6 binds to the opposite, basal end of the head domain, near its connection to the stalk (Hellert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hellert et al., 2019.

claim: 4B6 binds to the basal end of the SBV Gc head domain, near its connection to the stalk.
source: Crystal structures of the head domain in complex with two neutralizing murine mAbs, referred to as 1C11 and 4B6, have recently shown that 1C11 binds to the apical end of the head domain, near the N686 glycosylation site, and that 4B6 binds to the opposite, basal end of the head domain, near its connection to the stalk (Hellert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hellert et al., 2019.

claim: Binding of either 1C11 or 4B6 antibody is sterically incompatible with SBV Gc head domain trimerization.
source: Binding of either antibody is sterically incompatible with head domain trimerization, suggesting that neutralization may at least be partially mediated by destabilization of the spike's quaternary structure (Hellert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hellert et al., 2019.

claim: Neutralization by 1C11 and 4B6 may at least be partially mediated by destabilization of the SBV spike's quaternary structure.
source: Binding of either antibody is sterically incompatible with head domain trimerization, suggesting that neutralization may at least be partially mediated by destabilization of the spike's quaternary structure (Hellert et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Hellert et al., 2019.

claim: The Y541C mutation site in SBV Gc likely acts as a hinge allowing the head domain to adopt different orientations relative to the virion surface.
source: This site likely acts as a hinge allowing the head domain to adopt different orientations relative to the virion surface (Hellert et al., 2019), and antibody binding is thus expected to restrain the local mobility of the spike.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Hellert et al., 2019.

claim: Antibody binding to the Y541C site is expected to restrain the local mobility of the SBV spike.
source: This site likely acts as a hinge allowing the head domain to adopt different orientations relative to the virion surface (Hellert et al., 2019), and antibody binding is thus expected to restrain the local mobility of the spike.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural understanding.

claim: hIgG1 binds all mouse FcγRs with affinities that are similar to binding affinities of mouse IgG2a to the mouse receptors.
source: However, a recent study shows that hIgG1 binds all mouse FcγRs with affinities that are similar to binding affinities of mouse IgG2a to the mouse receptors (Dekkers et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dekkers et al., 2017.

claim: FcγR-mediated effector functions of the hIgG1Fc based bispecifics are expected to be maintained in mice.
source: Hence, FcγR-mediated effector functions of the hIgG1Fc based bispecifics are expected to be maintained in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data cited from Dekkers et al., 2017.
